## Why Does Selection Sometimes Fail? {background-color="#1B4332"}

*Pourquoi la sélection échoue-t-elle parfois ?*

::: {.notes}
Opening story, ~10 min total. Hook, then the heritability reveal,
then the breeder's equation, then the correlated-response twist, then
a second contrasting case (tomato flavor), then bridge explicitly to
today's heritability-of-floral-volatiles content.
:::

## A paradox in the dairy barn {.hook}

> For over 50 years, dairy breeders selected cows as hard as
> possible for one thing: milk yield. It worked spectacularly — yield
> climbed and climbed. 
>
> But fertility — how easily a cow gets
> pregnant again — got steadily *worse* over the same period, even
> though breeders wanted good fertility too. 
>
> Why would a trait move
> backwards under deliberate selection?

## 

- **Milk yield**: heritability h² ≈ 0.25-0.40 
- **Fertility** (e.g. daughter pregnancy rate): heritability h² ≈
  0.01-0.10

> **R = h² × S**
> Response to selection = heritability × selection differential

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This alone already explains why fertility barely improved
even when breeders started actively selecting for it in the
mid-1990s.

Decades of
  selection produced exactly what the breeder's equation predicts: a
  large, sustained response

 sometimes cited as low as **4%** — there's almost no
  additive genetic variance to select on at all


:::

## The breeder's equation

> **R = h² × S**
>
> Response to selection = heritability × selection differential

- **S** (how hard you select) is entirely under the breeder's
  control
- **h²** is not — it's a property of the trait, in that population,
  in that environment
- Push S as hard as you want: if h² ≈ 0, R ≈ 0 regardless

- Milk yield: selection produced what the breeder's equation predicts: a
  large, sustained response

- Fertility: Even under intense, sustained selection pressure, a trait with
  h² near zero simply **cannot respond** — the raw material isn't
  there

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is the single equation that makes the rest of today's
material legible - keep it visible/referenced for the floral volatile
heritability discussion later.
:::

## But fertility actually got *worse*, why?

## But fertility actually got *worse*, why?

- Low heritability alone only predicts **no progress**, not active
  decline
- The missing piece: milk yield and fertility are **negatively
  genetically correlated** — the same genes that push yield up tend
  to push fertility down
- One widely cited analysis attributes roughly **75% of a 37-day
  increase** in "days open" (time to successful rebreeding) to the
  *correlated* side-effect of selecting for yield — not a direct
  attack on fertility at all

**Selecting hard on one trait can drag a genetically correlated trait
along with it — for better or for worse.**

::: {.notes}
~2 min. This is the conceptual heart of today's "trade-offs" theme -
a correlated response can be positive (a free lunch: both traits
improve together) or negative (a trade-off: you can't have both).
Source: standard animal-breeding literature on Holstein fertility
decline, e.g. the Journal of Dairy Science 100-Year Review.
:::

## Tomato flavor:

> **Tomato flavor** also "failed" under 20th-century breeding — flavor
  compounds declined as shelf-life and fruit size were selected for

## Tomato flavor:

- Flavor compounds have real, measurable genetic variance

## Tomato flavor:
- Flavor compounds have real, measurable genetic variance
- Flavor is NOT under direct selection (selection on fruit size and shelf-life)
- **Resource-allocation trade-off** — bigger fruit dilutes
  a fixed pool of sugars and volatiles across more water and biomass,
  lowering concentration per unit weight


::: {.notes}
~2 min. Deliberately placed right after the dairy case for contrast.
Whether a trade-off comes from shared genes (pleiotropy, as in dairy
fertility) or from a tight physiological/resource constraint acting
on otherwise-independent traits (as in tomato flavor), the practical
consequence for a breeder - or for natural selection - is the same:
you cannot just add up selection on each trait separately. Klee and
colleagues have argued volatile compounds specifically may not share
the same yield trade-off that sugar content does - worth flagging as
an open, actively-studied question rather than settled fact.
:::

## Reasons for no desirable responses after selection

-  **Low heritability**
- **Genetic correlation / trade-off**

<!--
| | **Low heritability** | **Correlation / trade-off** |
|---|---|---|
| The problem | Not enough additive genetic variance to select on | Selecting trait A moves trait B too |
| Example today | Dairy fertility (h² ≈ 0.04) | Dairy fertility × yield; tomato flavor × fruit size |
| Direction | Only ever stalls progress | Can help (positive) *or* hurt (negative) |
-->

## Now you try it: four chemical ecology cases {.hook}

*À vous d'essayer : quatre cas en écologie chimique*

For each case, decide: **low heritability**, **genetic

1. **Glucosinolates in *Brassica*** — after just 3 generations of
   divergent artificial selection for leaf glucosinolate content,
   high- and low-selected lines had clearly diverged — but the
   high-defense lines also produced fewer flowers and seeds per fruit.
2. **Pheromone blend ratios in moths** — the ratio of two components
   in a sex pheromone blend rarely evolves independently, because
   both compounds are made by the same desaturase/reductase enzyme
   steps in one biosynthetic pathway.
3. **Floral scent in wild tobacco (*Nicotiana attenuata*)** — its
   night-time scent (dominated by benzyl acetone) attracts pollinating
   hawkmoths — but the *same* hawkmoth species also uses that scent to
   decide where to lay eggs, and the larvae then eat the plant.
4. **Cyanogenesis in white clover (*Trifolium repens*)** — populations
   are a patchwork of cyanogenic and non-cyanogenic plants that has
   persisted for decades, not swept to fixation either way.

⏳ Discuss in pairs, 3 minutes.

::: {.notes}
~1 min to set up, ~3 min discussion. Deliberately mixes one case that
is genuinely ambiguous/combined (case 1) and one that breaks the
two-bucket framework entirely (case 4), so students have to notice the
framework isn't exhaustive, not just pattern-match keywords.
:::

## Reveal: case 1 - glucosinolates {.smaller}

**Both at once.** Glucosinolate content *does* respond readily to
selection - real, substantial additive genetic variance, confirmed
across *Brassica* and *Arabidopsis*. But the high-glucosinolate lines
paid a measurable reproductive cost (fewer flowers/seeds per fruit) -
a genuine correlated trade-off between defense and reproduction
riding on top of a trait that is otherwise a textbook "selection
works" case.

**Not a failure of heritability - a cost that heritable selection
exposed.**

::: {.notes}
Source: divergent selection experiments on foliar glucosinolate
content in *Brassica rapa* (3-generation direct response, documented
fitness cost in flower/seed number); corroborating heritability and
QTL work in *Brassica oleracea* (highly heritable aliphatic
glucosinolate level, allelic variation at ~4 loci, including a
MAM-locus region).
:::

## Reveal: case 2 - moth pheromones {.smaller}

**Genetic correlation / pleiotropy.** When two pheromone components
share upstream biosynthetic enzymes, a mutation that shifts one
compound's abundance often shifts the other too - the blend *ratio*
is the functional signal (it's what distinguishes one species/race
from another to a male's antennae), so it can't easily be tuned one
compound at a time. This is a textbook case of pathway-level genetic
constraint in chemical communication, documented across several moth
systems (e.g. divergent pheromone races linked to shared
desaturase-pathway variants).

**Same mechanism as dairy yield/fertility - just enzymes instead of
whole-organism physiology.**

## Reveal: case 3 - wild tobacco scent {.smaller}

**Ecological trade-off, not a genetic one.** The scent (plus nectar)
that pulls in pollinating hawkmoths is read by the *same* insect
species for a second decision - where to oviposit - so one signal
serves two audiences with opposing consequences for the plant. A
California population with unusually low benzyl acetone, in a
high-herbivory area, hints that local herbivore pressure can shift
where the plant sits on this trade-off.

**The cost isn't paid through genetics (correlation) or physiology
(resource allocation) - it's paid because one signal is read by
multiple receivers with different interests.**

::: {.notes}
Source: Kessler, Baldwin and colleagues on *Nicotiana attenuata*
floral scent (benzyl acetone as dominant night scent, hawkmoth
pollination) and an eLife study manipulating scent and nectar jointly,
finding both increase pollinator-mediated outcrossing *and* hawkmoth
oviposition (nectar the stronger driver of the two). Caveat for
students: most direct evidence manipulates scent and nectar together,
not benzyl acetone alone - flag this as how real chemical ecology
data often arrives bundled, not cleanly separated.
:::

## Reveal: case 4 - clover cyanogenesis {.smaller}

**Breaks the two-category framework.** This isn't selection failing -
it's selection pulling in *different directions in different places*
(spatially varying selection) and staying there: cyanogenic plants are
better defended against herbivores/slugs, but the same cyanide-release
pathway damages the plant's own tissue after frost, so cold sites
favor non-cyanogenic plants. Neither allele wins everywhere, so the
polymorphism persists rather than going to fixation.

**A reminder: "heritability" and "correlation" aren't the only reasons
a trait doesn't evolve toward one fixed optimum - the optimum itself
can vary across the landscape.**

::: {.notes}
Classic case (Jones 1973 and extensive follow-up work) - genuinely
well-established, safe to present with confidence. Good moment to
explicitly say: today's two-category framework is a teaching
simplification, not the full story - flag it before moving to the
dedicated heritability content so students don't over-apply the
framework later.
:::

## Bridge to today

**Before we can ask whether floral scent can evolve under pollinator
selection, we need to know which of these traps it falls into - if
any.**
